prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B024 to B031, and I want to say why in terms of my own criteria rather than because five colleagues prefer it. The chair asked whether novelty was my only objection to the lattice clock. It was the main one, and the first-round exchange has largely removed it. Lindroth, Pearce, Olsson and Kroll each made the same analytical point from different directions: the 2005 comb prize supplied a way to count optical cycles, and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems, but neither solved the problem of interrogating very many neutral atoms for a long time without trap-induced shifts. The magic-wavelength condition solves exactly that, and it is the kind of simple, general mechanism I look for: the light shift of the two clock levels is made equal by choice of one parameter, so the perturbation cancels in the observable. That one idea is what moved stability, and not only accuracy, to the 10^-18 regime and opened the many-body clock physics in the lattice. It is a mechanism that is understood and not merely observed. It is also reproduced to the same level by several competing laboratories, the interpretation is not in dispute, and the credit for the idea and the first demonstrations (Katori) and the accuracy and many-body programme (Ye) is the cleanest on the shortlist. The fundamental-physics return I earlier undervalued, such as millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, is a real physical consequence and not only a smaller error bar. I would ask that the citation name the magic-wavelength lattice so that it is not read as a second comb prize.
statement.case_against: My reservations are narrower than before but not gone. First, the priority record outside the two names (Lemonde and the early SYRTE work, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley) is something I cannot verify from the files, and several colleagues rightly ask for a check before the final ballot. A two-name prize is only defensible if Katori's proposal and first demonstrations and Ye's accuracy and many-body programme are the decisive threads, as most colleagues assert. Second, a committee that reads Nobel's will strictly may still see this as an exceptionally good instrument rather than a discovery of something new in nature, and the formal redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Third, B024 still has the stronger conceptual novelty: a flat-band prediction from a continuum model followed by an unexpected experimental discovery that opened a new class of correlated matter. I do not think the unsettled pairing mechanism is a trivial detail, but I also do not think it is a reason to defer for ever, and I would expect B024 to be a strong candidate in a coming year once the superconducting state and the credit to the first experimental authors are clearer.

responses.point: Lindroth argued that the comb gives the means to count optical cycles whereas the lattice clock solves a different problem, interrogating many atoms for a long time without trap-induced shifts, and asked which part of the lattice-clock record I think is decisive for the omitted groups.
responses.response: You have persuaded me on the novelty question. I had treated the lattice clock as a refinement of a measurement line already honoured in 2005 and 2012. Your formulation shows it is a distinct mechanism: the magic wavelength cancels the differential light shift, which is what allows many atoms to be probed at once and so improves stability. That is the type of simple and general mechanism I trust. On your question about omitted groups, I think the decisive record is the sequence of Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice demonstrations, then the Ye-group accuracy and many-body work. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley appear to me as confirming and refining that line, but I cannot verify this from the files and I support your request that the record be checked before the final ballot.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asked whether I would accept B031 as a safe second choice if B024 lacks a majority, and noted that the difference between us is one of maturity rather than merit.
responses.response: Yes, and I go further than a second choice: I now put B031 first. You are right that by my own account the clock is mature and reproduced, and my usual standard is that a result should be understood and not only observed. Twisted bilayer graphene does not yet meet that standard for its superconducting phase, so applying my criterion consistently favours the clock. I do not withdraw my admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation, but I accept that the maturity gap is real and that waiting a few years costs B024 little. I also note your caveat on Higgs attribution: I still cannot support a configuration I cannot defend on a principled credit rule, so B005 remains outside my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that the pairing mechanism concerns only one phase, that the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle is robust and widely reproduced, and that leaving Bistritzer out of a 2011 two-author calculation is hard to defend.
responses.response: I agree with you on the science: the existence of flat bands and correlated states is robust, and the Cuprates comparison is fair, since we did not wait for a mechanism there. I also still think Bistritzer belongs with MacDonald if B024 is awarded, and I would not accept a two-name fallback on that side. Where I differ now is on weighing: even if the pairing question is only a detail, the first experimental author of the 2018 papers is outside any three-name credit, and that incomplete experimental credit is a problem that the clock does not have. That asymmetry, together with Lindroth's point on novelty, is what changes my first choice. I would keep B024 as my first alternative and would support it in a later cycle.

responses.point: Johansson pushed back on my ranking the clocks eighth as metrology, arguing that comparing clocks across a millimetre tests relativity and is access to new physics, not just a smaller error bar, and that B024 is premature on maturity and the missing experimental first authors.
responses.response: I accept the correction. My opening ranking undervalued the physics that a clock at 10^-18 makes accessible: gravitational redshift over millimetres, many-body spin-exchange effects inside the lattice, and sensitivity to variation of constants and to dark matter. That is the kind of experimental contact with fundamental questions I normally prize. I still share your caution about the omitted lattice-clock groups and agree with you that the right response is to examine the record explicitly rather than widen beyond three names.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that fundamental importance should outweigh clean attribution, that the Higgs is the clearest unrecognised discovery on the list, and that a clock prize would extend the 2005 and 2012 lineage rather than open something new.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs boson discovery is scientifically first-rate and I ranked it fourth for that reason. My difficulty is attribution and not merit: I proposed Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee in my opening, you proposed Gianotti, Jenni and Della Negra, and Pearce and Johansson proposed different sets again. I cannot say on scientific grounds which rule, founders or spokespeople, is correct, and I am not in a position to judge it as an outsider to particle physics. On your lineage argument, I now think it understates the novelty of the magic-wavelength mechanism, but I accept that the prize committee may reasonably weigh importance differently. If the committee finds a defensible Higgs credit rule before the vote I would reconsider it as a second choice.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley is consistent with a two-name prize for Katori and Ye; I have not been able to verify it from the files.
Whether the committee regards a precision-measurement invention as a discovery in the sense of Nobel's will, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes in adjacent areas.
Whether the superconducting state in twisted bilayer graphene will be understood well enough, and the first experimental authors' credit clarified, for B024 to be a robust candidate in a later year.
Whether a principled credit rule for the Higgs discovery (founders or spokespeople) can be agreed within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no collaboration with Katori, Ye or any other credited candidate on the shortlist. My Gothenburg physics environment overlaps with Johansson and Olsson at Chalmers, but I have no specific collaboration with them that would require recusal, and I record it for transparency.
